AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges
from Workflow OutcomesThanks: *These authors contributed equally to this work

Abstract

LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge’s prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge’s input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott’s π\pi) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent’s outcome labels, with 25% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped fail labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25% to 20%. Recalibrating that agent’s judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow (π\pi 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge’s input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

I Introduction

Coding agents now author code changes (diffs) at scale, and most of what they produce is not verifiable by a test: refactors, performance optimizations, cleanups and open-ended fixes. In an agent’s pipeline, an LLM judge [1] is an increasingly common quality-assurance step for such changes: it helps decide which diffs reach human reviewers. A judge, however, is only as good as its calibration (fitting the prompt to labels) for the task at hand: even strong judges are unreliable on objective correctness [2], and agreement with humans varies so much across evaluation tasks that no judge is a drop-in replacement [3]. Calibrating against manually labeled datasets is resource intensive, and the labels go stale whenever the agent, the model or the code distribution moves, so in practice many judge prompts are never validated at all. Keeping a judge trustworthy is therefore a life-cycle task: calibration must run unattended and be rerun whenever the agent it judges evolves.

The development workflow already emits labels continuously: tests pass or fail, and changes land or are abandoned. We expect merge and abandon outcomes to be most informative when the judge evaluates an automated system that produces changes, and our use case is consistent with this (Sec. IV-B). Outcome labels can still mislead a judge in two ways. The outcome may be decided by information the judge never sees, such as a hidden test, or by something other than the code, such as scope, process or a broken pipeline. A judge fitted to these labels learns to predict noise.

We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge’s prompt to reproduce outcome labels, together with an informed teacher that curates those labels before the loop sees them. The teacher reads exactly what the judge will read plus the outcome. It explains each label it keeps, and when the outcome cannot be explained from the judge’s view it abstains, removing the sample instead of inventing a label. Its abstention rate doubles as a monitoring signal: when the teacher abstains on many samples, the judge needs better inputs, not a better prompt. We contribute:

  • •

    The loop and the abstaining, explaining teacher (Sec. II), used as a quality-assurance component on an internal agent-evaluation platform.

  • •

    Calibration under trustworthy labels (Sec. III): on an execution oracle, calibration significantly improves a rubric judge beyond what threshold tuning achieves.

  • •

    Reducing label noise by abstention, and keeping a workflow’s judge current (Sec. IV): in a controlled noise test and on a performance-optimization agent’s merge/abandon labels, plus the recalibration of that agent’s judge after the agent evolved.

II Method

II-A Setting

We call a reviewable unit of code change a diff. A deployable judge sees a fixed view xx of a diff: its title, summary and code changes, plus a reference patch (Sec. III-B) or a test plan (Sec. IV). Each diff carries a label y∈{pass,fail}y\in\{\textsc{pass},\textsc{fail}\} from the workflow, such as an execution oracle or the diff’s terminal review status; the label source is pluggable, so manually curated labels work the same way. The goal is a judge prompt whose verdicts on xx reproduce yy on diffs it has not seen. The loop needs only the judge’s view of an output and an accept or reject outcome, so it applies to any agent whose outputs receive such outcomes.

II-B Calibration loop

The loop (Fig. 1) is an iterative optimizer over the judge’s prompt. The prompt plays the role of the parameters, agreement with the labels on the training split is the objective, disagreement analysis supplies the update direction, and a validation split decides when to stop. Each iteration runs the current prompt on the training split and scores its verdicts with Scott’s π\pi [4], which corrects raw agreement for the agreement expected by chance from the pooled verdict and label distribution, so a judge that always predicts the majority class scores at or below zero (−0.08-0.08 on our oracle test split). For every disagreement, an LLM (Claude Opus 4.7 in our runs) reads the judge’s verdict and reasoning next to the label and any teacher justification and proposes edits. The edits must be balanced, so every new reason to fail is paired with a reason to pass, which keeps the judge from drifting toward rejecting everything. A second call applies the edits under a length cap. For rubric judges, which emit a weighted score, the decision threshold is chosen on the training split. A separate validation split, never curated, selects the final prompt; the loop stops at a target agreement, when no disagreements remain, or at a maximum number of iterations (five in our runs, on training splits of 125 to 127 diffs). The agent’s patches are recorded once and replayed, so calibration never reruns the agent under test.

II-C The abstaining, explaining informed teacher

Before calibration, the teacher reviews each training sample. In this paper it sees exactly the judge’s view xx plus the label yy. It has three jobs. It explains the label, writing a justification grounded in xx; this is what the disagreement analysis uses to tell the rewriter why the judge was wrong. It may correct the label in either direction when xx clearly contradicts it, though in our runs it rarely did (2 of 512 merge/abandon diffs). And it abstains, returning skip when yy cannot be explained from xx; abstained samples are dropped from calibration and from disagreement analysis. By design the teacher prefers abstaining to a low-confidence flip, so it never invents a label it cannot support. The teacher thus performs outcome-aware filtering and explanation, loosely analogous to distillation with privileged information [5, 6]; reviewer comments, which our dataset builder already collects, would add genuine side information by showing why a diff was abandoned.

A label cannot be explained from the judge’s view when it is wrong, or when the view lacks the evidence for it. In the main oracle setting (Sec. III-B), both are less likely: execution outcomes make the labels reliable, and the judge also sees the reference patch, which helps explain why a patch fails. There, we calibrate on the labels directly.

III Calibration Under Trustworthy Labels

We first ask whether the loop works when the labels can be trusted, using execution outcomes as labels. This experiment serves two purposes: ground-truth labels let us validate the method before trusting it on noisier labels, and, because test coverage is uneven, a judge calibrated on the diffs that have tests can score similar diffs that have none.

III-A Setup: benchmark and splits

The benchmark is built from landed diffs in an industrial monorepo, each with fail-to-pass tests. One agent (Claude Opus 4.6) attempted 579 tasks; after dropping empty patches (trivial failures with no signal for a judge) we keep 417 records (353 pass, 64 fail). They are split by task into training (127, rebalanced to about 70/30 so the loop sees enough failures), validation (85) and test (85, with 13 failures); the last two keep the natural ratio of about 85/15. The other 120 records are surplus passes left out by the rebalancing. We calibrate two agentic judges (Claude Opus 4.8) that compare the agent’s patch with the production reference patch: a rubric judge that scores five weighted checks, and a pass/fail judge that returns a verdict. Tests are stripped from both patches, so neither judge sees the oracle. We use these labels directly, without the teacher (Sec. II-C).

III-B Result: calibration catches failures beyond threshold tuning

Calibration raised the rubric judge from π=0.36\pi=0.36 to 0.600.60 (Table I), and the threshold does not explain the gain. At the threshold chosen on the training split, the uncalibrated prompt reaches similar failure recall only by flagging four times as many good patches (pass recall 0.80 vs. 0.95), for π=0.33\pi=0.33; even the best threshold picked on the test set itself gives only 0.42. Against the train-threshold baseline the paired gain is +0.27+0.27 to +0.30+0.30 in π\pi, with the 95% bootstrap interval above zero and McNemar p≤0.013p\leq 0.013 in every replay; we report paired intervals rather than single point estimates, in the spirit of uncertainty-aware evaluation of AI products [7]. The uncalibrated pass/fail judge rarely failed a patch; calibration nearly doubled its failure recall (0.38 to 0.73) at the cost of precision (0.80 to 0.53), for π\pi 0.46 to 0.54. Paired by task against each uncalibrated replay, the calibrated judge’s single replay caught 3 to 4 failures that the uncalibrated judge missed, and missed none that it caught. Rubric replays are stable (π\pi standard deviation 0.018).

III-C Result: without the reference, failures are invisible

Without the reference patch, the judge’s view holds less evidence, so the teacher curates the training labels. The same loop then reached only π=0.35\pi=0.35 on the 85-task validation split (from −0.08-0.08 for the uncalibrated starting prompt, which passed everything), catching 5 of its 13 failures; because the teacher also set aside most training failures, the loop had few failures to learn from. To check whether the failures were visible at all, we ran the teacher retrospectively on the validation split, which calibration never curates. It abstained on 12 of the 13 failures and on none of the 72 passes, each time with the same reason: the patch reads as correct, and the failure lives only in the hidden tests. Abstention thus flagged the labels the judge’s view cannot explain, without the teacher seeing the tests itself.

To test whether people can see these failures, engineers reviewed 56 teacher-curated tasks blind to the outcome and to the teacher (25 abstained failures, 11 kept failures, 20 kept passes, drawn from the training and validation splits; two independent rating teams, about five minutes per task). Seeing only the title, summary and patch, they judged each patch correct, incorrect or undecidable. Both teams missed nearly all failures, whether the teacher had abstained on them (23 and 22 of 25 not called incorrect) or kept them (10 of 11 each); across both teams, 54% of failure ratings called the patch correct and 36% undecidable. They did better on passes, calling 12 and 9 of 20 correct. The judge’s inputs are thus not enough to see these failures, which is the condition the teacher’s abstention flags. Sec. IV-B shows that the teacher also separates visible failures from invisible ones. For the kept failures, the teacher, reading with the outcome in hand, cited specific defects, and 4 of 5 mechanically checkable claims held up. The two teams agreed on which outcomes they missed on 79% of tasks (κ=0.43\kappa=0.43).

IV Reducing Label Noise by Abstention, and a Calibrated Judge

IV-A Result: abstention reduces injected label noise

To measure noise reduction directly, we flipped 25% of the labels at random (fixed seed) in two settings and ran the teacher (Claude Opus 4.8) unchanged: the performance-optimization agent’s 185-diff calibration set (Sec. IV-B), where defects are often visible in the diff, and the 127-task training split of the reference-free oracle study (Sec. III-C), where failures are invisible from the patch. On the calibration set, the teacher set aside 13 of the 24 landed diffs relabeled abandoned but only 16 of the 73 genuinely abandoned ones (Fisher p=0.004p=0.004). Label noise fell from 24.9% to 20.4%; dropping the same number of labels at random within each label leaves 24.9% (p<0.001p<0.001). On the oracle split, noise fell from 25.2% to 14.0%, but the teacher set aside genuine failures nearly as often as flipped ones (20 of 27 vs. 19 of 21), so its gain matches a rule that drops every fail label. In both settings it abstained rather than relabeled (1 relabel in 185 labels, none in 127). It was also asymmetric: it kept most failing diffs labeled pass (19 of 22 and 10 of 11). Errors that look like success to a reader of the diff pass through. This preference is by design, set by the teacher’s prompt, to prioritize recall over precision of good diffs and can be tuned to the use case.

IV-B Result: the teacher abstains where abandonment is not in the code

We next apply the teacher to the labels it was designed for. The performance-optimization agent in our case study submits diffs for review; the label is the diff’s terminal status (landed == pass, abandoned == fail). What “abandoned” means depends on the pipeline: many diffs are abandoned while still drafts, largely after internal triage by the team operating the agent and before they are published for code review, while others are abandoned after a code reviewer has seen them. Review metadata fetched from the code-review system shows that most abandoned diffs were never published (Fig. 2).

We ran the teacher on the 512 terminal diffs of Fig. 2. The teacher sees the title, summary, diff and test plan plus the outcome. It abstained on 60% of diffs abandoned after review, 32% of drafts and 5.5% of landed diffs (Fisher p=10−5p=10^{-5} for after-review vs. drafts; Fig. 3). The pattern holds in the 327 new, uncurated diffs (60% vs. 37.5%, p=0.002p=0.002) and in the class-balanced calibration set (58% vs. 16%, p=0.003p=0.003), and a fresh teacher run agrees with the decisions logged during the original calibration on 112 of 125 diffs (κ=0.83\kappa=0.83). The gap points the same way before the judge became part of the internal triage workflow (39% vs. 23% on 200 abandoned diffs, p=0.10p=0.10, not significant) and after (71% vs. 45%, p=0.002p=0.002).

The teacher’s stated reasons show why. Abstained review-abandoned diffs read as “a clean, behavior-preserving code-motion optimization” with no defect visible in the diff; kept abandoned diffs cite visible problems, such as work relocated rather than removed, noise-level gains, or a summary that contradicts its own measurements. The teacher withholds labels where the reason for abandonment is not in the code, the same behavior as on the hidden-test failures of Sec. III-C. Reviewer comments support this reading. Among the diffs abandoned after review whose comments state a reason, the comments cite a problem visible in the diff for 13 of the 19 the teacher kept but only 14 of the 38 it abstained on (Fisher p=0.048p=0.048); the others cite duplicates, superseded work or a cleanup bot closing stale diffs.

IV-C Result: recalibration raises the judge’s recall

The agent’s initial judge (v1v_{1}) had been tuned on diffs from an earlier version of the agent’s workflow. We recalibrated it with AutoRefine (v2v_{2}, rubric judge, Claude Opus 4.8) on 125 training diffs from the calibration set, of which the teacher set aside 19, and selected the best iteration’s prompt on the 27 selection diffs (Fig. 2); v2v_{2} then replaced v1v_{1} in that internal workflow. The judge first ran in shadow mode to help the team triaging the agent’s diffs publish fewer bad diffs without losing good ones, so recall on landed diffs is the deployment metric, and a teacher that keeps pass labels (Sec. IV-A) protects it. Table II reports the held-out slices. On 43 diffs from the then-current distribution that were not used for training (26 of the 27 selection diffs, one lost to a v1v_{1} infrastructure failure, plus 17 test diffs), π\pi rose by a paired +0.31+0.31 (95% CI [0.03,0.61][0.03,0.61]) and recall on landed diffs rose from 12/20 to 18/20, the deployment target of 0.90; recall on abandoned diffs barely moved (11/23 to 12/23). The 17 test diffs, never used for training or selection, form the independent test: there π\pi rose from 0.16 to 0.51 (+0.35+0.35, CI [0.00,0.74][0.00,0.74]) and landed recall from 6/8 to 8/8, a small sample whose gain matches the 43-diff one. On 16 older test diffs, v1v_{1} stays ahead; because the test split mixes two distributions, we report its current and legacy slices separately. We checked that these older diffs come from an earlier version of the agent’s pipeline: 12 of the 16 were produced by three optimization workflows that account for only 3 of the 17 current diffs. We also checked whether v1v_{1}’s verdict, once visible to the triaging team, could have biased draft abandonment: 36 of the 43 evaluation diffs (and all 16 older legacy diffs) predate v1v_{1}’s verdict becoming part of the workflow and carry no v1v_{1} annotation, so v1v_{1} cannot have shaped their labels. On these 36 the gain is larger than on all 43 (+0.39+0.39, CI [0.10,0.70][0.10,0.70]; landed recall 9/15 to 14/15).

V Related Work

LLM judges. LLM-as-a-judge was validated against human preferences by Zheng et al. [1]; later work documents biases [8], weak performance on objective correctness [2], task-dependent agreement with humans [3], and pitfalls in how judges are validated [9].

Prompt and judge optimization. Prompts can be optimized without weight updates [10, 11, 12]. Closest to our work, AutoCalibrate [13] refines an LLM evaluator’s criteria and EvalGen [14] aligns evaluators with user grades, both against human labels. AutoRefine instead takes supervision from workflow outcomes and adds a teacher that explains or withholds each label; the optimizer itself is interchangeable.

Expert validation and uncertainty in AI engineering. Prior work motivates domain-expert oversight [15] and uncertainty-aware evaluation from stratified samples [7]; an independent, representative audit of production labels remains future work.

Weak supervision. Denoising labels from noisy sources is the core of weak supervision [16], which combines many noisy labeling sources rather than one teacher.

Oracles and SE for ML. For changes without tests, the judge acts as the oracle in the broad sense of the oracle problem [17], and keeping such ML components correct as data and systems change is a core concern of software engineering for ML [18].

Outcomes in software engineering. Pull-request acceptance and merged vs. abandoned changes have long been prediction targets [19, 20, 21]. There, the outcome is the target, and acceptance reflects many factors besides technical quality; here the outcome is a noisy label for calibrating a judge.

VI Lessons, Threats to Validity and Conclusion

Lessons for practitioners. (i) Recalibrate whenever the agent or its workflow changes: v2v_{2} wins on current diffs, while v1v_{1} still wins on the older diffs it was tuned on (Sec. IV-C). (ii) Use merge/abandon labels for judges of agent-written diffs, and check what a label means at each pipeline stage (a discarded draft is not a reviewer’s rejection); for human-written diffs, abandonment more often reflects scope or process, which the teacher can only set aside. (iii) Ask reviewers to say why they abandon a diff: a comment cannot make the diff judgeable from what the judge sees, but it would sharpen the teacher’s justification, which the disagreement analysis turns into new rules for the judge’s prompt.

Threats to validity. Construct: workflow outcomes stand in for code quality, and abstention can also drop useful samples, such as genuine failures that look clean. Internal: judge and teacher share a model family, which risks self-preference [8]; in our runs the teacher caught correct patches labeled fail but not failing patches labeled pass, and use cases that need the opposite should tune its prompt. External: all studies come from one source, and the merge/abandon study from one agent in use. Conclusion validity: samples are small, each calibration loop ran once per setting, and the human review covers 56 tasks with moderate agreement between the two rating teams.

Conclusion. AutoRefine calibrates a code judge from labels the workflow already produces, with a teacher that explains the labels it keeps and abstains on the ones it cannot explain. Under trustworthy labels, calibration raised a rubric judge’s π\pi from 0.36 to 0.60, beyond what threshold tuning achieves. On a performance-optimization agent, recalibration raised the judge’s π\pi from 0.16 to 0.51 on an independent held-out test. The teacher keeps labels it cannot explain out of calibration.
